sweep_summary: this search of works with stress in the title surfaced exactly one stress-titled work for Towa/Jemez, Bell 1993 'Jemez tones and stress' (CRIL 12: 26-34), which is already the catalog's deciding source. the open-access copy we hold (CU Scholar/OJS scan, image-only, scanned held by the project) was re-read in full; the deciding quotation is verbatim at sec. 10, p. 32 (page scan checked: running head 32), and the article concludes that word-initial syllables carry stress independent of tone, with compounds stressed once on the first syllable and a few Spanish loans treated as having an extraprosodic first syllable. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding; no new source supersedes it. The DOI landing page (journals.colorado.edu, 200) confirms the bibliographic record (author, title, journal, 1993, DOI, PDF URL); scholar.colorado.edu could not be reached by automated download. PDF and scanned were copied into and. Nothing remains to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title's list; the previously filed works still to obtain (Yumitani 1998 KU dissertation, ProQuest/a Harvard login only; Martin 1964 UNM MA thesis, not located) are outside this search of works with stress in the title's title list and unchanged.

Matches the catalog's classification fixed-strict initial.

tone_statements.quote: All the other languages have phonemic tones or stresses--sometimes both of them. [...] As for Tanoan languages, Sandia has three tones (high, mid, low) and three stresses (primary, medial, weak), while Jemez has two tones (high, low). Santa Clara possesses stress and pitch accents (high, mid, low, falling, weak), and only syllables with a strong stress make pitch distinctions. Finally, Taos has three phonemic tones (high, normal, low). In summary, although there is yet much to be known about suprasegmentals of these Pueblo lahguages, it seems that some kind of tones play an important function in the majority of the languages.

tone_statements.summary: Two phonemic tones, high vs low (secondhand, after Martin 1964).

sources.citation: Bell, Alan. 1993. Jemez Tones and Stress. Colorado Research in Linguistics 12(1): 26-34. Boulder: University of Colorado (Graduate Working Papers; ISSN 1937-7029). DOI 10.25810/vt8v-3v40.
sources.quote: 10. INITIAL SYLLABLES ARE STRESSED. Initial syllables of words (including compounds) are metrically strong, since they are the only syllables which require a H tone (either alone or as part of a HL Falling tone), and which permit long vowels. The longer duration, more peripheral vowel quality, and slightly higher pitch of initial High toned syllables compared to noninitial High syllables, to the extent that these preliminary results are not unrepresentative, point to the extra effort of a stress gesture as at least part of the source of the perceived prominence of initial syllables. I conclude from all this that stress is part of the prosody of Jemez, and that initial prominence is not a derivative property of the H and F tones.

sources.note: Word-initial syllable is stressed (fixed initial), on instrumental evidence (duration, vowel quality, pitch of initial vs noninitial H syllables; one speaker, elicited data, explicitly preliminary).
